q1: SELECT b.name AS bar, COUNT(DISTINCT f.drinker) AS num_drinker, AVG(s.price) AS avg_price, (SELECT f1.drinker FROM frequents AS f1 WHERE f1.bar = b.name ORDER BY f1.times_a_week DESC, f1.drinker ASC LIMIT 1) AS most_reg_drinker FROM bar AS b LEFT JOIN frequents AS f ON b.name = f.bar LEFT JOIN serves AS s ON b.name = s.bar GROUP BY b.name ORDER BY num_drinker DESC, b.name ASC
q2: WITH max_drinker AS (SELECT f.bar, f.drinker, f.times_a_week FROM frequents AS f JOIN (SELECT bar, MAX(times_a_week) AS mt FROM frequents GROUP BY bar) AS md ON f.bar = md.bar AND f.times_a_week = md.mt) SELECT f.bar, COUNT(DISTINCT f.drinker) AS cd, AVG(s.price), md.drinker FROM frequents AS f JOIN serves AS s ON f.bar = s.bar JOIN max_drinker AS md ON f.bar = md.bar GROUP BY f.bar, md.drinker ORDER BY cd DESC, md.drinker ASC

explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they handle the selection of the most regular drinker. Q1 uses a subquery to find the most regular drinker for each bar, while Q2 uses a CTE to achieve the same result. The difference arises when there are ties in the number of times a drinker visits a bar in a week. Q1 will return the drinker with the lexicographically smallest name in case of a tie, whereas Q2 will return the drinker with the highest number of visits in case of a tie.
counterexample_dsp: Create a scenario with two bars, 'Bar A' and 'Bar B', and three drinkers, 'Drinker 1', 'Drinker 2', and 'Drinker 3', where 'Drinker 1' visits 'Bar A' 3 times a week, 'Drinker 2' visits 'Bar A' 2 times a week, and 'Drinker 3' visits 'Bar B' 3 times a week. 'Drinker 1' and 'Drinker 3' have the same number of visits to 'Bar A' and 'Bar B' respectively, but 'Drinker 1' has a lexicographically smaller name than 'Drinker 3'.
